phrases: At forty-one thousand feet over Canada, a brand-new Boeing seven sixty-seven goes completely silent.
Both engines, gone.
Sixty-nine people on board.
No fuel, almost no instruments, and about seventeen minutes to find somewhere to land.
This is the Gimli Glider, and the machines that brought it home.

chapter: A brand-new jet with blank gauges

phrases: July the twenty-third, nineteen eighty-three.
Air Canada Flight one forty-three is getting ready to fly from Montreal to Edmonton.
The seven sixty-seven is one of the airline's newest planes, and one of the first to measure its fuel in kilograms instead of pounds.
But tonight, the fuel gauges in the cockpit are blank.
A faulty sensor has knocked them out.
By the rules, the plane should never have been cleared to fly. But it was.
So the crew does it the old way.
A stick is dipped into the tanks, the depth is read, and a chart turns it into litres.
The trip needs twenty-two thousand, three hundred kilograms of fuel.
To turn litres into weight, you multiply by the fuel's density.
They used one point seven seven.
But that's pounds per litre, not kilograms.
The right number was about zero point eight, so every litre was counted as more than twice its real weight.
Every number on the sheet looked right.
But the tanks held less than half the fuel the flight needed.
At a stop in Ottawa, they dip the tanks again, and make the same mistake again.
And with the gauges dead, nothing in the cockpit can warn them.
Over Red Lake, Ontario, a warning chimes.
Low fuel pressure in the left engine.
The captain turns for Winnipeg.
Then the left engine stops.
A few minutes later, the right engine stops too.
The engines also make the plane's electricity, so the glass screens in the cockpit go dark.
Even the transponder dies, so controllers on the ground can no longer see how high they are.
And a warning sounds that nobody on board had ever heard before.
All engines out.
The seven sixty-seven is now a very heavy glider.
But its controls are moved by hydraulic pressure, and the pumps were powered by the engines.
So, from the belly of the plane, a small propeller drops out into the wind.
The ram air turbine.
The rushing air spins it, and it drives a hydraulic pump, just enough to move the controls.
Just enough.
No flaps, no slats, and the plane gets harder to steer as it slows down.
With only backup instruments, the crew works out the glide by hand.
The backup instruments don't even show how fast they're sinking.
In ten nautical miles, they lose five thousand feet.
At that rate, Winnipeg is too far.
They would hit the ground first.
First officer Maurice Quintal remembers an old air force base where he once served.
Gimli.
What nobody in the cockpit knows is that part of the old base is now a racetrack.
And today, there's a car race on it.
As they line up, they're too high and too fast.
With no engines, there's no second try.
But Captain Bob Pearson is also an experienced glider pilot.
He crosses the controls, one wing down and the opposite rudder, so the jet flies slightly sideways.
The whole side of the plane hits the wind like a brake.
It drops fast, without speeding up.
The landing gear falls out by gravity.
The main wheels lock.
The nose wheel doesn't.
The seven sixty-seven hits the runway.
The nose collapses and scrapes along the concrete, slowing it down.
The main wheels straddle a guardrail down the middle of the runway, and the jet grinds to a stop, short of the people at the race.
A small fire at the nose is put out by racers with hand extinguishers.
All sixty-nine people survive.
Ten have minor injuries, mostly from the evacuation slides.
The plane was repaired, and flew for almost twenty-five more years.
Pearson and Quintal were later given an award for outstanding airmanship.
Everyone called it the Gimli Glider.
When it finally retired, pieces of it were turned into luggage tags.
One wrong number nearly brought it down.
A dropped propeller, a glider pilot's trick, and an old runway brought it home.
What would you have done at forty-one thousand feet?
Tell me in the comments.
